en: The paper that started it all was about translation. Today's big chatbots threw away half of its design.
From Lecture 2 of Professor Yufei Ding's CSE 291P at UC San Diego.
The paper: Attention Is All You Need, 2017. Its model, the Transformer, was built to translate: a sentence in, its translation out.
The encoder reads the sentence; the decoder writes the translation.
Picture a team at one desk: a reader and a writer.
He reads a sentence in a made-up language. She writes the translation: I am a student.
Before 2017, the best translators were mostly recurrent networks.
A recurrent network reads one word after another, like a whisper passed down a line: one step per word.
The 2017 paper dropped recurrence and kept only attention. Hence the title.
Attention is a round table. Each word asks: which of the others are like me? It gathers from them, weighted by that, and updates itself.
Unlike the whisper line, all the words do this in the same step, so a GPU can work on them at the same time.
The reader uses attention: every word can look at every other word, before and after it.
Models read text in tokens: words or pieces of words. Professor Ding:
Writing, though, is still one word at a time, and each new word joins the input for the next.
Before each word, she reads his notes on the whole input. That is cross-attention.
That's the 2017 team. Professor Ding's advice for reading an older paper:
So, what would you cut?
Most of today's large chat models that publish their design keep only the decoder. They fired the reader.
Slide 11 of the lecture shades the cut in red. Delete the encoder. The cross-attention has nothing left to look at, so it goes too.
What stays: the decoder alone. It's called decoder-only.
Alone, the writer keeps the rule she always had: a card hides the rest of her strip.
Each word may look at itself and the words before it, never ahead. That's called masked, or causal, attention.
So how does she translate now? Write the request at the start of her page. It came first, so the card never hides it, and she simply continues the text.
What does she lose? Try this: The bank was full of fish.
When she reaches “bank”, the card hides the fish. Money, or river? The reader saw the whole sentence at once.
Why read both ways at all? Professor Ding:
Looking only backward can hurt on some understanding tasks.
So why accept a less exact model? Professor Ding's slide 12 keeps the books.
First gain: one stack instead of two.
The numbers a model learns are called parameters, or weights. Each half is a stack of layers; two stacks carry more: about 1.5 to 2 times, the slide estimates.
By our count, that cut takes the 2017 base model from about 63 million parameters to about 38 million: about 40% fewer.
Second gain: practice.
To learn translation directly you need pairs: a sentence and its translation. That's paired data. The 2017 model learned from about 4.5 million sentence pairs.
A next-word model, like our writer, can learn from any text: hide the next word, guess it, check.
GPT-3 read about 300 billion tokens; Llama 3, about 15 trillion.
One honest limit. A 2022 study found next-word models best right after training on plain text, but two-stack models ahead after extra training on many tasks.
And two-stack models still show up in translation.
So which is better? Professor Ding asks the question students ask:
Accurate: the team, reading both ways. Simple: the lone writer, any text.
Remember episode one: scale changes what models can do. The simple design that scales won, for now. Nobody has proven it is the best design.
Professor Ding's verdict:
Most of today's big chat models kept only the writer: she never peeks ahead, but any text is practice.
Next time you read an older paper, try Professor Ding's test: guess what comes after it.
